issues.legal_issue: A possession application is not defective merely because it omits the words that the lease was in writing when, read as a whole, it sufficiently refers to the written lease.
material_facts: The possession application referred to the lease between the parties but did not expressly state that the lease was in writing.
The lease was in fact written, and the application read as a whole implied that fact.
The application was amended to add the omitted words, and the tenant argued that the amendment was made after the limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The application was sufficient without amendment, so the limitation question concerning the amendment did not arise for decision.
issues.legal_principle: Pleadings are not statutes and should be read as a whole with common sense rather than as verbal formulae. An omission is not fatal where the material fact is adequately conveyed by the pleading. The Court did not decide the separate limitation question.

predicates.rent_control_possession_execution: The proceeding seeks possession through an execution procedure under rent-control law.
predicates.application_identifies_written_lease_in_: The application refers to the lease in a way that, read as a whole, conveys that the lease was written.

issues.definition: When a rent-control possession application in an execution proceeding conveys in substance that the lease was written, it is sufficient without an amendment adding those words.

issues.legal_issue: The special possession procedure for a letting for a limited period applies only when its essential statutory conditions, including temporary non-requirement of the premises and residential use, are satisfied.
material_facts: The premises had been let on successive occasions with permission under the special procedure.
The premises were being used to run a school, although the latest lease described the accommodation as required for residential purposes.

The Court considered the statutory purpose of making otherwise unused residential accommodation available for a limited period without allowing the special procedure to circumvent ordinary eviction protections.
issues.conclusion: The special procedure is confined to a genuine letting for a particular limited period for residential use, with the required prior permission and a period agreed in writing; absence of any essential condition means the procedure does not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 is an exception to the general restrictions on eviction under sections 14, 19 and 20 and must be kept within its narrow scope. The Court applied the mischief-rule approach associated with Heydon's Case to prevent circumvention of rent-control protections. Section 21 requires that the landlord not require the premises for a particular period, that the letting be for residential use, that the Controller's permission be obtained, and that the period be agreed in writing.

rule.if: section_21_special_possession_case and landlord_can_spare_premises_only_temporarily and letting_is_for_residential_use and controller_permission_obtained and letting_period_agreed_in_writing

predicates.section_21_special_possession_case: The proceeding seeks possession under a special procedure for a letting for a limited period.
predicates.landlord_can_spare_premises_only_tempora: The landlord genuinely does not require the premises during a defined limited period and requires them thereafter.
predicates.letting_is_for_residential_use: The premises are let to be used as a residence.
predicates.controller_permission_obtained: The Controller has granted permission before the letting under the special procedure.
predicates.letting_period_agreed_in_writing: The landlord and tenant have agreed in writing on the period of the letting.

issues.definition: The special possession procedure applies when the case concerns that procedure and the premises are genuinely available only temporarily, are let for residential use, and the required permission and written agreement on the letting period exist.

issues.legal_issue: The Controller must independently examine whether the essential conditions for special permission are met, even when the landlord and tenant jointly apply.
material_facts: The landlord and tenant had jointly applied for permission on successive lettings.
The Court found that formal assertions by both parties do not establish that the landlord genuinely required the premises only after a limited period or that the letting was for residential use.
The Controller's permission enables an exceptional possession procedure that could otherwise be used to bypass ordinary eviction protections.
issues.conclusion: The Controller must make such inquiry as is appropriate and satisfy himself that the landlord genuinely does not require the premises for the specified limited period and that the letting is for residential use; a joint application does not remove that duty.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the Controller performs an important regulatory function on behalf of the community. The mandatory conditions for permission cannot be reduced to formal averments, and the Controller must inquire into the genuine limited-period non-requirement and residential nature of the letting.

predicates.section_21_permission_application: An application seeks permission for a letting under a special limited-period possession procedure.
predicates.landlord_asserts_temporary_nonrequiremen: The landlord states that the premises are not required for a particular limited period.
predicates.proposed_letting_is_residential: The proposed letting is stated to be for use as a residence.

issues.definition: When permission is sought for a residential letting on the basis of temporary non-requirement, the Controller must inquire into whether those essential conditions are genuine.

issues.legal_issue: A party may challenge the validity of a special possession sanction at the execution stage by showing that mandatory conditions were absent or that the sanction was procured by fraud or collusion.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession through execution of a sanction granted under the special procedure.
The tenant was permitted to plead and prove that the sanction was a make-believe, vitiated by fraud or collusion, or that the conditions required for a valid sanction were not present.
The Court stated that the sanction is presumed regular, but that the presumption does not bar a challenge at execution.
issues.conclusion: The executing court may examine whether the essential conditions for the sanction were actually fulfilled and may treat the sanction as invalid if they were not; the tenant may raise and prove such a challenge at execution.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 imposes mandatory conditions for the special possession remedy. The Controller's sanction is presumed regular, but a party may prove that the conditions for validity were absent. A sanction procured by fraud or collusion cannot stand, and the executing court may determine its validity within the scope of execution objections. The Court rejected the contrary approach discussed in Kasturi Lal.

rule.if: section_21_possession_execution and party_challenges_sanction_validity and (mandatory_conditions_absent or sanction_procured_by_fraud_or_collusion)

predicates.section_21_possession_execution: The proceeding seeks possession by executing a sanction granted under a special limited-period letting procedure.
predicates.party_challenges_sanction_validity: A party raises a challenge to the validity of the sanction in the execution proceeding.
predicates.mandatory_conditions_absent: The conditions essential to a valid sanction were not in fact fulfilled.
predicates.sanction_procured_by_fraud_or_collusion: The sanction was obtained through fraud or collusion.

issues.definition: In an execution proceeding under the special possession procedure, a challenge supported by absent mandatory conditions or fraud or collusion permits the executing court to treat the sanction as invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Estoppel cannot validate a proceeding under a public-protection statute when mandatory statutory conditions are absent, particularly where fraud or collusion is established.
material_facts: The tenant had entered the premises following permission granted under the special procedure.
The Court considered the contention that the tenant's acceptance of the letting prevented a later challenge to the permission.
The Court held that fraud or collusion and the absence of mandatory conditions could be raised notwithstanding the tenant's earlier participation.
issues.conclusion: Estoppel cannot be invoked to validate a sanction that fails mandatory statutory conditions, and a tenant's acceptance of the premises does not bar a challenge to the legality of the sanction.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory proceeding subject to mandatory conditions imposed for public policy cannot be validated by estoppel when those conditions are absent. The Court relied on the principle that a person cannot use estoppel to prevent performance of a statutory duty, and on the stated rule that a judgment obtained by fraud or collusion may be treated as a nullity, cited from Halsbury's Laws of England. It also held that there is no estoppel against a statute where fraud or collusion and the public purpose of the law are involved.

rule.if: statutory_sanction_dispute and mandatory_conditions_absent and (fraud_or_collusion_established or public_protective_duty_breached)

predicates.statutory_sanction_dispute: The dispute concerns the validity of a sanction granted under a statute imposing mandatory conditions.
predicates.mandatory_conditions_absent: Conditions made mandatory for a valid sanction were not fulfilled.
predicates.fraud_or_collusion_established: Fraud or collusion in obtaining the sanction has been established.
predicates.public_protective_duty_breached: A statutory duty imposed to protect a public purpose has not been performed.

issues.definition: Estoppel cannot validate a statutory sanction when mandatory conditions are absent and fraud, collusion, or breach of a public-protective duty is established.
